records.name: Guam
records.summary:
An unincorporated US territory, so the 2025–26 federal turn — marker/document policy, TSA screening, the trans military-exclusion order — lands hard on an island whose economy and society carry a large permanent US military presence. Local law partly cuts the other way: Guam was the first US territory to recognise same-sex marriage (2015, after a local lesbian couple sued over a denied licence), its statute book bars employment discrimination including gender identity, and federal hate-crime coverage has applied since 2009.

Academic Pacific-identity surveys record indigenous Chamorro understandings of gender diversity, and a local advocacy scene maintains ID-documents guidance for residents. The synthesis for a visitor: real written protections and a quiet, integrated public record, against military-community conservatism, federal volatility amplified by the base, and small-island visibility where an outed stranger is noticed.

sources.claim: Advocates for Trans Equality 'Know Your Rights' guide to US airport security (TSA): body-scanner flags, pat-downs, documentation mismatches, and how to request alternative screening - relevant to Guam as a US territory under TSA procedures.

Human Rights Watch (Mar 2026): 'US State Revokes Gender-Affirming Identification' — Kansas voids birth certificates and driver's licenses not matching sex assigned at birth; US document-policy context relevant to US territories.
University of Hawaii Manoa library research guide on Pacific sexual identity - resources on sexual and gender diversity across the Pacific, including Chamorro contexts relevant to Guam.

NPR (Jan 2025): Trump's executive order could ban transgender troops from the US military - speaks of transgender identity in 'sweeping and dismissive terms'; directly affects Guam given its large US military presence.
TransEquality (Advocates for Trans Equality) ID Documents Center page for Guam - information on changing gender markers on Guam identity documents.

The Guardian (June 2015): Guam became the first US territory to recognise same-sex marriage, after Loretta Pangelinan and Kathleen Aguero sued when denied a marriage license; marriages from the following Tuesday.

records.name: Guyana
records.summary:
Guyana is dangerous for trans visitors — one of only five Western-Hemisphere countries still criminalising same-sex conduct (buggery carries life imprisonment on paper, though rarely enforced). The IACHR heard evidence in November 2024 of severe violence against trans women: 69 cases of violence against trans women documented 2018–2022, in a country of under a million people. Police fail to investigate anti-LGBT violence; there is no anti-discrimination legislation (the UN Human Rights Committee called for it in April 2024) and no legal gender recognition.

Cross-dressing was decriminalised after a 2018 CCJ ruling (McEwan v AG), removing the most direct trans-expression statute, but the climate and investigative failure keep risk high. Georgetown has a small organised community (SASOD).

sources.claim: Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): Guyana is one of only five Western Hemisphere countries still criminalising consensual same-sex conduct - Sections 352-354 of the Criminal Law Act ('gross indecency', attempted buggery, buggery with life imprisonment). Rarely enforced but fuels stigma. In 2025 five of six election-contesting parties, including the ruling party, supported decriminalisation. Cross-dressing was criminalised until 2018 (Section 153(1)(xlvii)), targeting trans people; no legal gender recognition.

Stabroek News (Nov 2024): at an IACHR hearing requested by a local group, testimonies on gender-based violence in Guyana were heard; the Inter-American Commission called on Guyana to take urgent action.

BBC News (March 2017): Guyana's transgender activists fight the 1893 colonial-era cross-dressing law (Summary Jurisdiction Act, s.153(1)(XLVII)); trans woman Petronella Trotman was stabbed and attacked with bottles, then told by the magistrate to 'dress like a man' - 'We live in a very homophobic society.'

Stabroek News (Nov 2018): the Caribbean Court of Justice ruled in favour of Guyanese transgender women (Quincy McEwan, Angel Clarke, Peaches Fraser et al.) - the cross-dressing law is unconstitutionally vague and violates freedom of expression; Section 153(1)(XLVII) struck from the laws of Guyana.

PinkNews (March 2017): transgender activists in Guyana fight archaic transphobic laws - Trotman's scissors attack, the magistrate ordering her to 'dress like a man', and the 124-year-old cross-dressing law blocking justice.

News Room Guyana (May 2019): SASOD's Joel Simpson documents police using discriminatory laws to extort LGBT persons - men in 'compromising positions' threatened with arrest to extract bribes; those who do report face further discrimination at police stations.

records.name: Hong Kong
records.summary:
A special administrative region running its own legal system under a constitutional settlement: trans claims here have been fought in court more than legislated. Same-sex conduct is not criminalised, and the apex court in 2023 ruled full sex-reassignment surgery must not be a precondition for changing the gender marker on the compulsory identity card — reversing a 2019 high-court loss in the same litigation. Beyond the card, however, recognition still runs on surgery; and where the executive has chosen, it has chosen against: in September 2025 the legislature voted down the government's own registered-partnerships bill 71–14 after court deadlines, so relationship recognition and any SOGI equality ordinance remain absent.

Corporate visibility invites backlash (a bank's rainbow installations drew a homophobic campaign in 2016), and open activism operates in a space tightened since the 2020 security law. Visitor arithmetic: no criminal law, dense urban anonymity, a functioning marker-change route on cards — inside a system that still demands surgery for most recognition and whose politicians recently voted inclusion down.

sources.claim: AP (Feb 2023): 'Hong Kong transgender men win appeal over status change' — the Court of Final Appeal rules full sex-reassignment surgery should not be a prerequisite for changing the gender marker on official identity cards, a far-reaching win in the Henry Tse case.

PinkNews (Feb 2019): Hong Kong's High Court ruled against three trans men (Henry Tse, Q and R) seeking legal gender change without full confirmation surgery - Judge Thomas Au called full surgery the 'only objectively ascertainable criterion'; the men had already changed legal gender in Britain; lawyers called the requirement 'out of proportion'.
Hong Kong Free Press (Dec 2016): opinion piece on HSBC's rainbow-lion statues and the homophobic backlash they provoked - the social climate around corporate LGBT visibility in Hong Kong.

Hong Kong Court of Appeal judgment (Leung TC William Roy v Secretary for Justice, CACV317/2005, Sept 2006): landmark ruling on whether the Crimes Ordinance's buggery provisions unjustifiably discriminate against gay men - the court examined whether facially neutral laws can be discriminatory; key precedent for equal age of consent.

freshness.fact: LegCo VETOED the government's registered-partnerships bill 71–14 (Sept 2025) after the Sep-2025 court deadline; legal gender recognition still requires full sex reassignment surgery

records.name: Honduras
records.summary:
Honduras is dangerous for trans visitors. It is the site of the hemisphere's defining transfemicide case: Vicky Hernández, a trans woman and activist shot dead in 2009, whose case reached the Inter-American Court of Human Rights — which in 2021 found the Honduran state itself responsible for her death and for failing to investigate it as a bias crime. The ruling ordered reforms (including legal gender recognition, which Honduras has partially implemented), but violence against LGBT people remains at levels Amnesty called “epidemic,” driving mass asylum-seeking.

Nothing criminalises being trans, and the Vicky Hernández ruling created formal obligations; a name-change process exists. But gangs, security forces, and social actors all contribute to a documented pattern of violence against trans women in particular, and prosecution remains rare.

For a visitor: no legal exposure, but outing-violence probability is among the highest in the hemisphere outside Brazil/Mexico.

sources.claim: Wikipedia article on transfemicide: definition, legal views, and regional patterns (US, Mexico, Argentina, Colombia) - background concept for Honduras's extreme violence against trans women.

Latin America Working Group Education Fund report 'Left in the Dark': violence against women and LGBTI persons in Honduras and El Salvador ranks among the world's highest; trans women are especially targeted and face major obstacles to justice; impunity for sexual and gender-based crimes is driven by under-reporting, lack of training, insufficient resources, and institutional failure.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying Reuters feature covers Central America's LGBT people being terrorised at home and fleeing for their lives.

HRW report (May 2009) 'Not Worth a Penny': Human Rights Abuses against Transgender People in Honduras - police rape, assault and extortion of trans people, the shape of transgender lives in Honduras, and relevant domestic laws.

GlobalGayz archive of Honduras news and reports (2004-2011): the 2005 gay-marriage/adoption ban, the Donny Reyes case, murders of trans people, post-coup violence against LGBT people, and the killing of young LGBT activists amid impunity.

US State Department 2021 Human Rights Report for Honduras: significant human-rights issues include violence and threats against LGBTQI+ persons, extrajudicial killings, torture, corruption, and lack of accountability for gender-based violence.
Washington Blade (Sept 2017): a transgender woman ran for Honduras's Congress - a rare openly trans political candidacy.

records.name: Croatia
records.summary:
Croatia is broadly workable with a cleaner documented traveler-axis profile than its Balkan neighbours: no mob violence, trans-tourist rape, police-brutality case, or foreign-trans-detention case surfaced in research. The Dalmatian coast's international-tourism culture (Dubrovnik, Hvar, Split) is broadly open, and Zagreb has the Balkans' most established gay scene.

The framework is weaker than Western Europe's: legal gender recognition (available since 2015) is partial and not self-ID (it covers only some documents), there is no marriage equality (a 2013 constitutional ban), and an anti-gender movement is active. A 2024 prosecution of a host who refused to accommodate a gay couple shows enforcement works, and the President was formally criticised for outing a minister.

The Catholic-conservative climate is more marked outside the main tourist areas. Croatia is in the EU and Schengen, so border friction for most travellers is low.

sources.claim: Zagreb Pride documentation report (2018) on Croatia's implementation of CoE Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)5: hate-crime legislation and under-reporting of homophobic/transphobic crimes, hate speech case studies, freedom of assembly, legal gender recognition, same-sex partnership recognition, employment discrimination, and compiled hate-crime data with case studies.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024) chapter on Croatia: a Zadar prosecutor charged a man for refusing a gay couple's accommodation booking (2018 incident); anti-gender disinformation escalating - a Croatian Parliament session on 'Gender Ideology' featured speakers spreading misinformation with no LGBTI organisations invited; the first Pula Pride march faced disruption the day before.

Croatian legal journal article (2026, in Croatian) by Nenad Igrec: 'Search of Persons - Specific Characteristics of Conducting Searches of Transgender, Trans, and Gender Non-Conforming Persons' - academic analysis of how personal searches should be conducted for trans and gender-nonconforming people under Croatian law.
US State Department 2021 Human Rights Practices report for Croatia (archived): official assessment including treatment of LGBTI persons.

Wikipedia overview: same-sex activity legal since 1977; life partnership since 2014; gender identity and expression sections; hate-crime legislation; police cooperation; Pride events including Zagreb, Split, Osijek, Karlovac, Pula and the Balkans Trans Inter March; LGBT tourism.

Intrepid Travel country guide: Croatia 'widely accepts' LGBTQIA+ travellers — legal since 1977, with recent life-partnership and protection laws — but PDA may draw unwelcome responses outside big cities and gay venues are virtually non-existent outside Zagreb.

European Commission legal experts' country report on non-discrimination in Croatia (2024, reporting period 2023): transposition and implementation of the EU equality directives, including SOGI grounds.

CroL (May 2014, in Croatian): Split got an LGBT Centre - the second in Croatia and first in Dalmatia; the 4th Split Pride (7 June 2014) announced with the slogan 'Potpuna ravnopravnost' (Full equality), repeated from the previous year to signal LGBT people's unequal position in Croatia.

CroL (Oct 2014, in Croatian): the LGBTIQ+ centre Druga Rijeka was presented in Rijeka - founded from the local community's need for more active LGBTIQ+ development in Primorsko-goranska county, networking with national and international organisations.

records.name: Haiti
records.summary: Haiti is dangerous for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is legal, but the state has effectively collapsed: gangs control most of Port-au-Prince, the police are outgunned, and mob violence against perceived LGBT people is documented. There is no LGR, no protection infrastructure, and no functioning judiciary. The trans-specific risk is inseparable from the generalised collapse — outing in gang-controlled territory can be lethal.

sources.claim: Washington Blade (Nov 2019): a prominent Haitian LGBTQ activist was found dead - part of the pattern of violence against LGBT people in Haiti.

HRW World Report 2018, Haiti chapter: political instability hindered meeting basic needs; includes a Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity section documenting violence and discrimination against LGBT Haitians.

freshness.fact: Not a criminal offence (consensual adult), but trans people exposed to vagrancy-law fines and zero protection/hate-crime coverage — current summary matches; only cited 'source' was a homepage (dead link) and should be replaced.

records.name: Hungary
records.summary:
Hungary is in a fast-improving post-Orbán transition. The most acute traveler-facing risk — the 2025 Pride ban with facial-recognition identification of attendees — has stopped: the 2026 Budapest Pride was held freely. Péter Magyar's Tisza party won a supermajority in April 2026, ending 16 years of Orbán rule, and the EU's top court has ruled that Hungary's 2021 "child protection" law breaches EU values (handing the new government a repeal mandate).

However, the Orbán-era laws remain on the books: a total ban on domestic legal gender recognition (2020), the "child protection" content law, and a constitutional amendment banning LGBTQ public events. The structural weakness that has not changed with the election is detention: a German court in 2025 blocked the extradition of a non-binary person to Hungary because of prison conditions and the person's identity, and watchdogs report transphobia in prisons with a "culture of silence."

Bathrooms are unrestricted, there is no criminalisation of trans identity, and the Schengen border poses no trans-specific entry friction. Social hostility lingers outside Budapest, but the state-led demonization that characterised the Orbán years has ended.

sources.claim: NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying France24 piece (June 2026) covers LGBTQ rights in Hungary after the election - 'we are very hopeful that changes will be made'.

AP (Jun 2026): 'Hungary holds its first Budapest Pride in the post-Orbán era' — tens of thousands march in the 31st Budapest Pride, the first since Viktor Orbán was voted out, against the backdrop of his era's anti-LGBT laws.

The Dissident analysis (April 2026) by Alejandra Caraballo: what Hungary's election (Tisza's 138 seats, ending Orbán's rule) actually means for LGBTQ people - a return to democratic baseline, not liberation. Details the 'constitutional architecture of erasure': the May 2020 total ban on legal gender recognition (redefining 'nem' as immutable biological sex), forcing trans Hungarians to carry mismatched documents.

Wikipedia overview: same-sex activity legal since 1961; legal gender change de facto impossible since 2018 and explicitly illegal since 2020; the 2021 child-protection law restricts 'promotion' of homosexuality/gender change; the 2025 Pride ban; discrimination protections and public opinion.

BBC (April 2026): the European Court of Justice ruled Hungary's anti-LGBTQ laws (2021 'child protection' ban on 'promotion' of homosexuality or gender change to under-18s) violate EU rules and - unprecedentedly - the founding values of Article 2 of the EU Treaty; the law stigmatised trans and non-heterosexual people by associating them with paedophilia. Ruling came nine days after Hungarians voted to end Orbán's rule.

niHaplus (April 2026): Budapest Pride spokesperson Johanna Majercsik says anti-queer laws can be repealed with a two-thirds majority; Tisza's 138 seats give it that power, but its silence on LGBTQ+ rights raises questions; the most urgent issue is restoring the right of assembly (2025 Pride ban). Recaps the 2012 two-sex constitutional amendment, 2020 adoption ban, and the 2021 Child Protection Act conflating LGBTQ+ people with child abusers.
NOTE: This is a German Federal Constitutional Court press release (2025), not about Hungary; appears to have been included in the source list in error or as comparative context.

Hungarian Helsinki Committee / Háttér Society national report (2025) on LGBTIQ detainees in Hungary, part of the EU-funded 'Strengthening the rights of LGBTIQ detainees in the EU' project - the situation and rights of LGBTIQ people in Hungarian detention amid the current legal and political climate.

HRW World Report 2025 Hungary chapter: the government's assault on rule of law continued in 2024, including a law giving a government-appointed body broad powers to harass civil society and independent media; includes a Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity section.

ECJ judgment C-247/23 Deldits (13 March 2025): on GDPR accuracy and rectification of gender-identity data in Hungarian public registers - the Court addressed Hungary's administrative practice of demanding proof of gender-reassignment surgery before correcting data that was incorrect from the time of inclusion.

BuzzFeed News (April 2020) by Patrick Strudwick: Hungary's new law will end legal gender recognition - 'It's just horrible,' a trans woman told BuzzFeed News; 'I don't want to lose good people because of this' - trans Hungarians speak out as the decree banning gender changes was published.

freshness.fact: 2020 legal-gender-change ban stands (explicitly illegal); 2021 'child protection' law in force; NEW: March 2025 law bans organising/participating in Pride — Budapest Pride permit denied 3 June 2025

records.name: Indonesia
records.summary:
Indonesia is a dangerous destination for trans visitors — with a directly documented trans-traveler death in custody and a presidential decree classifying LGBTQ+ as a national security threat. Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard trans activist from Peru, died in Bali police custody in 2022 after arrest at Bali airport on his honeymoon (family alleges police beating; police deny violence).

In Aceh province, Sharia law criminalises same-sex relations with public caning (applies to all persons in Aceh, including tourists). A new penal code effective January 2026 effectively criminalises all same-sex conduct nationally. President Prabowo in October 2025 classified "promotion of LGBTQ+ culture" as a national security threat alongside terrorism — and vigilante mob attacks on trans women escalated after this decree (10 attacks documented in Bogor between March and July 2026). Police conduct discriminatory raids on gay gatherings (75 arrested in Bogor in June 2025).

BUT: Bali is a major tourist hub where many trans visitors enter discreetly without incident; Indonesia has no death penalty; and Rodrigo's death is disputed (police deny violence) rather than clearly documented state torture.

sources.claim: NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying Reuters report (Aug 2022) covers Indonesian police denying violence in the death of Harvard trans activist Rodrigo Ventocilla in Bali.

Harvard Crimson (Sept 2022): the mother of Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla - a 32-year-old Peruvian trans man and Harvard student - alleges he was arrested at Bali airport on drug charges, subjected to extortion (demands rising from $100,000 to $200,000), and died three days later in hospital while in police custody during his honeymoon.
The Diplomat (Aug 2026): Indonesia's transgender community faces growing repression - vigilante mobs attacking trans people as the government takes steps to codify anti-LGBT provisions.

ABC News (Aug 2026): analysis of attacks on trans women in Indonesia after a rule deemed them a 'threat' - trans women who were previously able to appear in public have become afraid; the attacks did not appear suddenly but build on longer trends.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying Reuters report (Feb 2025) covers Aceh province publicly caning two men for a same-sex relationship.

Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): the new penal code in force from 2 January 2026 penalises all consensual extra-marital sex (2 years), effectively criminalising same-sex relations since marriage is unavailable (complaint-based enforcement); the vague 2016 National Pornography Act has been used to target LGBTIQ people - 2025 police raids on 'gay parties' detained 56 in Jakarta, 75 in Bogor, 34 in Surabaya; online LGBTIQ content blocked.
Human Dignity Trust country profile: two provinces of Indonesia (Aceh and South Sumatra) criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women; national-level provisions target morality.

Amnesty International (June 2025): police raided a privately rented villa in Bogor described as a 'gay party', arresting 75 people (74 men, 1 woman); Amnesty called it 'a blatant violation of human rights and privacy that exemplifies the hostile environment for LGBTI people in Indonesia' and demanded release and accountability.

Human Rights Watch (Jul 2026): 'Indonesia: Surge in Abuse Against LGBT Students' — documented surge in abuse of LGBT students by authorities and institutions amid criminal-code expansion and campus purges.

HRW report (Aug 2016) 'These Political Games Ruin Our Lives': Indonesia's LGBT community under threat - 70 interviews; documents the anti-LGBT cascade starting with the higher-education minister's campus ban call, the defense minister calling LGBT activism 'more dangerous than a nuclear bomb', and resulting legislative proposals threatening LGBT Indonesians' rights and safety.

freshness.fact: New national penal code EFFECTIVE 2 January 2026: criminalises sex outside marriage (≤1 yr) and obscenity articles explicitly cover same-sex acts; first enforcement — 25 sentenced May 2026
